10.6. Exact Symbolic Calculus🔗

10.6.1. Verified Exact Symbolic Computation🔗

An exact residual proof often ends with a cancellation. To establish A(x)/B(x)=C(x) on a domain \Omega, we can normalize A(x)-B(x)C(x) to zero and prove that B(x)\ne0 throughout \Omega. Polynomial arithmetic can settle the first question; a sign, interval, or root-exclusion argument can settle the second. The domain determines where we may use the resulting equality.

The normalization and polynomial-root certificates of the exact core cover conditional cancellation, real powers and exponentials, exact polynomial division, and Sturm chains. The calculus bridges use such identities to justify derivatives and antiderivatives.

The core expression type is an inductive syntax tree indexed by its variable type. It contains rational constants, arithmetic operations, natural powers, real powers with an arbitrary real exponent (Mathlib's Real.rpow), trigonometric functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, square roots, and the inverse tangent, sine, and cosine. Evaluation uses Lean's total real functions. A separate validity predicate records sufficient conditions for their analytic rules: a nonzero denominator or logarithm argument, a positive square-root argument or power base, and an inverse sine or cosine argument different from \pm1. These conditions are needed by the calculus bridges; an equality about total values need not require them.

Schematically, the reflected language and its semantics are

e ::= q\mid x_i\mid \pi\mid \mathrm e \mid -e\mid e_1\mathbin\circ e_2\mid e^n\mid e_1^{\,e_2} \mid \sin e\mid\cos e\mid\arctan e\mid\arcsin e\mid\arccos e \mid\exp e\mid\log e\mid\sqrt e, \qquad \operatorname{eval}: \operatorname{Expr}(\iota)\to(\iota\to\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R.

Here \circ\in\{+,-,\times,/\}, the exponent n of e^n is a natural number while e_2 in e_1^{\,e_2} is an arbitrary expression, and rational literals with zero denominator are rejected by the well-formedness layer.

If the executable normalizer reduces an expression to literal zero, evaluating the original expression in any real environment gives zero. The computation therefore proposes a normal form, while this theorem is the kernel-checked semantic justification.

\operatorname{normalize}(e)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall\rho,\ \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)=0.

Proof for Theorem 10.2
uses 0

The normalizer is accompanied by an invariant equating evaluation of each intermediate form with evaluation of the input. Specializing that invariant to a returned literal zero identifies the original value with the evaluation of zero, hence with zero in every environment.

Rational cancellation and other conditional rewrites return the nonzero conditions they require. Under those conditions, reduction to zero again implies equality of the original real expression.

If normalization returns a zero expression together with side conditions S, then

\operatorname{normalizeWithSide}(e)=(0,S) \land\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)=0.

Every checked symbolic transformation is recorded by one route type. A SideClaimRoute stores the source and target expressions, the list of expressions that must not vanish, and a proof that the target and source evaluate equally wherever that list holds; a positivity requirement is encoded as the nonvanishing of a square root. An unconditional transformation is the same object with an empty list of assumptions.

For a route with source l, target r, and assumption list S,

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(r,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(l,\rho), \qquad S=[\,]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall\rho,\ \operatorname{eval}(r,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(l,\rho).

The side-conditioned pipeline contains a pass for the algebra of real powers and of the exponential, which it treats as the power of \mathrm e. Inside a product or quotient all powers of one base collect into a single power, nested powers flatten, powers of products distribute, exponents are put into a polynomial normal form, and a literal exponent is read back as a natural power, a reciprocal, or a square root. Each rewrite that Mathlib states for a positive base records the positivity of that base as a condition unless the base is structurally positive (a positive numeral, \pi, \mathrm e, an exponential, or a product of these); rewrites valid for the total Real.rpow, and the exponential identities, record nothing.

Writing (e',S) for the output of the pass on e,

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e',\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(e,\rho).

Proof for Theorem 10.5
uses 0

Each local rewrite uses the corresponding identity for real powers, square roots, or exponentials under its recorded positivity conditions. The bottom-up traversal retains every condition from the rewrites it applies. Induction over the traversal composes the local evaluation equalities into the equality for the whole tree; when the expression contains no power atom the pass returns it unchanged.

Exact interval evaluation encloses the value of a sparse rational polynomial at every real point of a rational panel. The root checks first try the centred form, the exact Taylor shift of the polynomial to the midpoint of the panel bounded term by term over its radius, and use termwise evaluation when the centred interval does not exclude zero. This theorem is the semantic basis for both root exclusion and derivative-sign checks.

x\in[a,b] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(x)\in\operatorname{enclosure}(p,[a,b]).

Proof for Theorem 10.6
uses 0

Termwise evaluation encloses each monomial with interval multiplication and natural powers and combines the terms with interval addition. The basic interval operations preserve membership, so induction over the sparse term list shows that the real polynomial value lies between the computed rational endpoints. For the centred form, write p(x)=\sum_k c_k(x-m)^k with the exact shifted coefficients c_k, where m is the midpoint and r the radius of the panel. Since |x-m|\le r, an even power (x-m)^k lies in [0,r^k] and an odd one in [-r^k,r^k], so every term lies in a rational interval and their sum encloses p(x). The enclosure returns one of these two sound intervals.

Proof for Theorem 10.7
uses 0

Sound interval evaluation places every p(x) in the computed range. The Boolean root-free test proves that zero is outside that range. Therefore no enclosed value can equal zero.

For example, on [2,3], interval arithmetic gives x^2-1\in[3,8]. This one enclosure proves that the denominator x^2-1 never vanishes there and also gives 1/(x^2-1)\in[1/8,1/3]. The nonvanishing fact justifies an exact cancellation; the two numerical endpoints control the size of the reciprocal. Exact reasoning and CEGA draw on the same domain information.

Proof for Theorem 10.10
uses 0

Use the checked monic decomposition to rewrite a hypothetical root equation. If |x| were at least the computed coefficient bound, the leading term would strictly dominate the sum of all lower-degree terms, contradicting that their sum is zero. Hence every root lies inside (-B,B).

Understanding a root certificate.

The isolated root need not be rational. A root atlas identifies it by a rational interval and a uniqueness theorem, which is often exactly what a PDE side-condition proof needs. The covering and uniqueness theorems of the RootAtlas and GlobalRootAtlas interfaces can discharge nonvanishing, domain, and monotonicity side conditions in later symbolic or PDE arguments. Those theorems have the same form whether an atlas was assembled from interval exclusion, Sturm subdivision, or both.

The Cauchy root bound in detail.

For a polynomial with rational coefficients, write it in monic form

p(x) = s \cdot \left(x^n + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k x^k\right),

where s \neq 0 is the leading scalar. The checked bound is

B = 1 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |a_k|.

A CauchyBoundCertificate stores only the decomposition fields (scale s, degree n, and the lower-degree tail). The bound B is computed from that tail. An independent checker validates:

  1. the scale is nonzero;

  2. every exponent in the tail is strictly below n;

  3. the sparse identity p = s \cdot (x^n + \text{tail}) holds after normalization.

When n=0, the checked tail is empty and p=s\ne0, so there are no roots. For n>0, the soundness proof (abs_lt_bound) proceeds by contradiction. If |x|\ge B and p(x)=0, dividing by s gives x^n=-\text{tail}(x). Since |x|\ge B\ge1, each lower-degree term satisfies |a_k||x|^k\le|a_k||x|^{n-1}. Hence

|x|^n\le\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|a_k|\right)|x|^{n-1}.

Dividing by the positive factor |x|^{n-1} gives |x|\le\sum|a_k|<B, a contradiction. The Lean proof implements this leading-term estimate with exact sparse evaluation and cancellation by the checked nonzero scale.

Example: isolating roots of x^2 + x - 1.

Consider the polynomial p(x) = x^2 + x - 1. A hand calculation shows the certificate data; the generator may choose different split points.

  1. Cauchy bound. In monic form the tail is x - 1, whose coefficient absolute values sum to 1 + 1 = 2. The checked bound is B = 1 + 2 = 3, so all roots lie in (-3, 3).

  2. Square-free reduction. The gcd of p and p' = 2x + 1 is 1, so p is already square-free and its radical is p itself.

  3. Sturm chain construction.

    • S_0 = x^2 + x - 1,

    • S_1 = p'(x) = 2x + 1,

    • Euclidean division gives S_0 = (\frac{x}{2}+\frac14)S_1 - \frac54, so S_2 = \frac54, a nonzero constant.

    The terminal polynomial S_2 = 5/4 has zero derivative and nonzero value, hence is globally nonzero (proved using the mean value theorem).

  4. Variation counting. At x = -3, the signs are (+, -, +), giving two sign changes. At x = 3, they are (+, +, +), giving none. The drop V(-3) - V(3) = 2 confirms that p has exactly two distinct real roots.

  5. Bisection. At x = 0, the signs are (-, +, +), giving one sign change. Thus V(-3) - V(0) = 1 and V(0) - V(3) = 1. The intervals (-3,0) and (0,3) each contain exactly one root.

  6. Atlas assembly. The global root atlas records the two isolated intervals, together with the checked Sturm certificate that proves their root counts.

The Sturm chain algorithm.

A Sturm chain for a polynomial p is a sequence S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_m satisfying:

S_0 = p, \quad S_1 = p', \quad S_{i-1} = Q_i S_i - S_{i+1} \quad (i = 1, \ldots, m-1),

where the last element S_m is a nonzero constant. This signed Euclidean remainder sequence is the ordinary Euclidean algorithm with the sign of each remainder reversed. The certificate checker (SturmCertificate.valid) validates every recurrence by exact polynomial arithmetic, independently of the generator that proposed the chain. The variation count V(c) is the number of sign changes in (S_0(c),S_1(c),\ldots,S_m(c)), zeros omitted; Sturm's theorem turns its drop between two endpoints into a root count.

The subdivision certificate.

A Sturm subdivision is a binary tree of rational intervals over a search interval, such as the Cauchy-bounded [-B,B]: every leaf has Sturm count at most one, and every split is at a rational point that is not a root. SymLean checks such a tree when a caller supplies it and has no generator for it; the root and sign commands use their own root-cover search and root-list checkers. Leaves whose Sturm count is one are the isolated root regions.

Sparse polynomial representation.

The polynomial subsystem uses Verified.Expr.Alg.MvPoly n, a raw list of rational coefficient–monomial pairs. A monomial is a function \text{Fin}(n) \to \mathbb{N} recording the exponent of each variable. The type permits repeated monomials and zero coefficients. The executable normalization combines terms, removes zeros, and orders the result without changing the polynomial's value.

Interpreting these lists as Mathlib polynomials over \mathbb Q preserves evaluation. Importing a Mathlib multivariate polynomial and exporting it again returns the original polynomial. In the other direction, different lists can represent the same polynomial, so a raw list need not equal its own round trip.

Key operations include:

  • Euclidean division: exact quotient and remainder satisfying p=qs+r for univariate polynomials.

  • Square-free factorization (squareFreeFactors?): a Yun-style candidate generator proposes factors indexed by intended multiplicity. Its output is a proposal; the semantic contract belongs to the radical certificate built from it.

  • Rational factors (RationalFactorization.split): linear and quadratic factors are kept; x is split off by exact division while it divides a factor of degree three or more; any other factor of degree three or more is split only if a supplied provider proposes proper factors whose product is the original factor. Otherwise it stays whole. Rational integration uses the list as a proposal and checks its final primitive by differentiation.

  • Exact evaluation (evalRat): evaluates at rational points with exact arithmetic, used for sign determination in Sturm chains.

  • Interval evaluation (evalInterval): rigorous enclosure of the polynomial's range on a rational panel.

uses 0

Along an interval containing no endpoint root, sign variation is locally constant except when crossing a root of p. The signed Euclidean recurrence shows that noninitial chain entries cannot create a net jump, while each distinct root of p decreases the variation by one. Summing the jumps from a to b gives the root count.

Sturm counts certify unique-root intervals and exact root counts for a checked subdivision tree. An accepted finite subdivision therefore projects to the same root-atlas interface used by interval and monotonicity certificates.

For each accepted node N with interval I_N,

N.\mathrm{rootCount} =\#\{x\in I_N^\circ\mid p(x)=0\},

and every leaf with count one projects to an \exists!\,x\in I_N,\ p(x)=0 certificate.

Proof for Theorem 10.16
uses 0

Apply the Sturm count theorem at every node. A node of count zero is root-free; a node of count one contains a root and cannot contain two distinct roots. For a split node, additivity of root counts over its adjacent children preserves the parent's exact count. Structural induction over the accepted subdivision tree therefore produces the root atlas.

The isolation certificates combine square-free reduction, a Sturm subdivision, transport back to the original zero set, and a checked rational Cauchy outer bound. GlobalPolynomialIsolationCertificate.valid checks every stage, and the noncomputable toGlobalRootAtlas projection then yields a global atlas covering every distinct real root; a nonzero constant has an empty atlas. SymLean checks these certificates when a caller supplies them and has no generator for them.

The final global contract is

p(x)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists R\in\mathcal A.\mathrm{rootRegions},\ x\in R,

with each root-bearing region carrying a unique-root theorem.

Scope of the exact core.

The decision procedures of the exact core work inside its reflected real language, with rational polynomial coefficients. A bounded search that returns none has found no supported certificate within its budget; the statement itself may still be true.

10.6.2. Symbolic Calculus and Analytic Bridges🔗

For a scalar field u, the coordinate derivative is \partial_i u(x)=Du(x)[e_i]: evaluate its Fréchet derivative on the ith basis vector. A symbolic derivative must recover this same linear approximation. The partial-derivative bridge proves that it does, under the domain conditions of the expression being differentiated. For example, \partial_x\log(x^2+y^2)=2x/(x^2+y^2) is valid whenever (x,y)\ne(0,0); neither coordinate has to be nonzero on its own.

uses 0

Structural induction on the expression constructs its Fréchet derivative using the analytic sum, product, quotient, power, and elementary chain rules. The validity hypotheses discharge each rule's domain conditions. Evaluating the resulting continuous linear map on e_i gives exactly the evaluated symbolic derivative, hence the stated coordinate identity.

The validity predicate that justifies one symbolic derivative also certifies regularity of every order. At a point where ValidAt holds, evaluation of a reflected expression is C^m for every smoothness order m, the analytic order included, because each constructor is interpreted by an elementary function that Mathlib proves smooth of every order away from its singularities; the On and global forms assume validity at every point of the set or the space. The theorems are stated for the two conventions of the theorem-facing tactics, functions on \mathbb R^n and functions on \mathbb R with frozen parameters, and they are what cas applies to a DifferentiableAt, Differentiable, ContDiffAt, ContDiffOn, or ContDiff goal:

\operatorname{ValidAt}(x,e) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^\sharp\text{ is }C^m\text{ at }x \qquad\text{for every }m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,\infty,\omega\}.

Proof for Theorem 10.19
uses 0

Structural induction on the expression. Constants and coordinate projections are smooth; sums, products, and negations preserve ContDiffAt; quotients, logarithms, square roots, real powers, and the inverse sine and cosine are smooth at every point satisfying the validity clause of their constructor, by Mathlib's ContDiffAt lemmas for the elementary functions and the field operations; the remaining elementary functions are smooth everywhere. The derivative bridge also gives differentiability, and the set and global forms quantify these pointwise statements over their domain.

At a point where the scalar inputs being differentiated are valid, the coordinatewise bridge gives gradient, divergence, and three-dimensional curl formulas. The Laplacian bridge additionally assumes validity of every first symbolic partial at that point. Hessians, Jacobians, symmetric gradients, tensor divergence, and vector Laplacians use the same finite-indexed construction. In particular, (\nabla_{\mathrm{sym}}e)^\sharp(x)=\nabla(e^\sharp)(x), (\Delta_{\mathrm{sym}}e)^\sharp(x)=\Delta(e^\sharp)(x), (\operatorname{div}_{\mathrm{sym}}F)^\sharp(x)=\operatorname{div}(F^\sharp)(x), and (\operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{sym}}F)^\sharp(x)=\operatorname{curl}(F^\sharp)(x).

Proof for Theorem 10.20
uses 1

For each coordinate, Theorem 10.18 identifies evaluation of the reflected partial derivative with the corresponding analytic derivative. The reflected gradient is the vector of these coordinates, divergence is their finite sum, the Laplacian is the sum of the diagonal second derivatives, and curl is the stated alternating combination. Function extensionality and finite-sum congruence assemble the coordinate identities into the four displayed operator identities.

For the Laplacian, applying the first-derivative identity only at x would not suffice: two functions can agree at one point and have different derivatives there. Validity persists on a neighborhood of x, so the analytic first partial and the evaluated symbolic first partial agree throughout that neighborhood. Their derivatives at x therefore agree. Validity of the first symbolic partial justifies the second application of the derivative bridge. These are sufficient conditions on the intermediate formulas; the largest domain of smoothness can be bigger.

uses 1

For momentum component i, assume ValidAt at x for u_i and p. The Navier–Stokes bridge also assumes validity of every first symbolic partial of u_i; the conservation bridge assumes validity of every flux component. These give the stationary Euler and Navier–Stokes momentum residuals and the divergence-form conservation residual. Incompressibility is a separate equation. The undifferentiated viscosity and source terms need no validity hypotheses for these identities. Componentwise, the Euler bridge gives R_i^{E}(x)=\sum_j u_j(x)\partial_j u_i(x)+\partial_i p(x)-f_i(x), while the Navier–Stokes bridge adds -\nu(x)\Delta u_i(x) and the conservation bridge gives R^{C}(x)=\sum_i\partial_i F_i(x)-f(x).

Normalize each reflected residual, rewrite its differentiated components using Theorem 10.20, and identify the transport term with Theorem 10.21. The remaining sums and products evaluate definitionally.

The viscosity term here is specifically -\nu(x)\Delta u_i. For a variable coefficient this differs from divergence-form diffusion:

-\nabla\cdot(\nu\nabla u_i) =-\nu\Delta u_i-\nabla\nu\cdot\nabla u_i.

The extra term vanishes for constant viscosity. Keeping the exact operator visible matters when applying a residual bridge: a certificate for one of these expressions says nothing about the other.

uses 0

Rewrite the analytic residual as the evaluation of the lowered residual, using the analytic side conditions. ClosedResidualVanishesAt is exactly the assertion that this evaluation is zero, so it finishes the proof. A side-aware normalizer is one way to supply that vanishing proof after its denominator and branch conditions have been discharged.

The integration entry point accepts a candidate F only after checking that \operatorname{diff}_iF-f normalizes to zero. Its certificate records requirements for the primitive, the integrand, and the conditional cancellations used in that check.

Fix a coordinate line \gamma(s)=x+s e_i. At each point where those requirements hold, the evaluated primitive has derivative f^\sharp(\gamma(s)). If they hold for every s\in[\min(a,b),\max(a,b)], then

\int_a^b f^\sharp(\gamma(s))\,ds =F^\sharp(\gamma(b))-F^\sharp(\gamma(a)).

The interval hypothesis is Set.uIcc a b in Lean. It includes both endpoints and every point between them, regardless of their order. Validity of the integrand supplies continuity and hence interval integrability; validity of the primitive supplies the derivative needed by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Every search method uses this same certificate. At the reflected API, IntegrationCheck.certifyCandidate? takes the coordinate, original integrand, and proposed primitive explicitly, so it can check a candidate without running primitive search. The ordinary interval tactic uses this boundary for a supplied function or a common function reconstructed from the requested endpoint difference. It reflects the integrand and candidate over one parameter table, so each coefficient has the same meaning in both expressions. Checking a candidate against its own derivative would not establish the requested integral.

For substitutions, the proportionality checker validates its proposed factor with Theorem 10.3. Polynomial, rational, substitution, and integration-by-parts passes only propose candidates. The integration checker validates the symbolic derivative identity with Theorem 10.3. Under the certificate's requirements, Theorem 10.18 turns it into an analytic derivative along \gamma. The interval-wide requirements also make the evaluated integrand continuous there, so the fundamental theorem gives the endpoint difference.

The differentiation rule tree in detail.

DiffRule names the differentiation rules, and DiffDerivation records their application to an expression. For an expression e and variable index i, this tree connects the raw derivative e.diff i to the analytic partial derivative. Its rules are:

  • Constant rule. Every rational literal, \pi, and \mathrm e differentiates to zero: \partial_i c = 0.

  • Variable rule. A coordinate x_j differentiates to the Kronecker delta: \partial_i x_j = \delta_{ij}.

  • Sum, difference, and negation. These distribute linearly: \partial_i(e_1 \pm e_2) = \partial_i e_1 \pm \partial_i e_2.

  • Product rule. For e_1 \cdot e_2: the derivative is (\partial_i e_1) e_2 + e_1 (\partial_i e_2).

  • Quotient rule. For e_1 / e_2 with e_2 \neq 0 at the evaluation point: the derivative is ((\partial_i e_1)e_2 - e_1(\partial_i e_2))/e_2^2.

  • Natural power rule. For e^n: the derivative is n \cdot e^{n-1} \cdot \partial_i e.

  • Real power rule. For e_1^{\,e_2} with e_1 > 0 at the evaluation point: the derivative is (\partial_i e_1)\, e_2\, e_1^{\,e_2-1} + (\partial_i e_2)\, e_1^{\,e_2} \log e_1, the two terms of Mathlib's HasDerivAt.rpow; a literal natural exponent is lowered to the natural power rule instead.

  • Transcendental chain rules. Each elementary function composes with the inner derivative \partial_i e:

    • \partial_i(\sin e) = (\cos e)(\partial_i e),

    • \partial_i(\cos e) = -(\sin e)(\partial_i e),

    • \partial_i(\arctan e) = (\partial_i e)/(1+e^2),

    • \partial_i(\arcsin e) = (\partial_i e)/\sqrt{1-e^2} and \partial_i(\arccos e) = -(\partial_i e)/\sqrt{1-e^2} (requiring e \neq \pm1),

    • \partial_i(\exp e) = (\exp e)(\partial_i e),

    • \partial_i(\log e) = (\partial_i e)/e (requiring e \neq 0 under Mathlib's total real logarithm),

    • \partial_i(\sqrt{e}) = (\partial_i e)/(2\sqrt{e}) (requiring e > 0).

The raw derivative is simplified by evaluating constant arithmetic, eliminating multiplication by zero or one, and removing addition of zero. These transformations preserve its value. A theorem may request a form that this simplifier does not reach, such as a factored heat-kernel derivative or a square-root expression needing (\sqrt u)^2=u. The derivative tactic then tries the side-conditioned normalizer, whose real-power and square-root rules identify the two forms under the recorded conditions.

Example: differentiating \sin(xy).

Consider the expression e = \sin(x \cdot y) with variables x = x_0 and y = x_1 in \mathbb{R}^2. Differentiating with respect to x_0:

  1. The outermost constructor is sin, so the sine chain rule applies.

  2. The inner expression is x_0 \cdot x_1, which uses the product rule.

  3. Differentiating x_0 gives 1 (variable rule, Kronecker delta).

  4. Differentiating x_1 with respect to x_0 gives 0 (variable rule).

  5. The product rule yields 1 \cdot x_1 + x_0 \cdot 0.

  6. The chain rule produces \cos(x_0 x_1) \cdot (1 \cdot x_1 + x_0 \cdot 0).

  7. The simplifier reduces this to x_1 \cos(x_0 x_1).

The bridge theorem then proves \partial_{x_0}[\sin(xy)](p) = y\cos(xy) at every point p = (x,y), as an identity in Lean's real analysis library.

Supported antiderivative patterns.

The bounded antiderivative search IntegrationPlanner.candidateWithFuel? combines seven mechanisms.

Polynomial integration. Sparse multivariate polynomials are integrated term by term. Each monomial c \cdot x_i^k integrates in coordinate i to c \cdot x_i^{k+1}/(k+1). The sparse representation avoids allocating zero coefficients.

Calibrated substitution. For an integrand f(x), the planner collects a list of substitution primitives. These include \log g for quotients by g, inverse-power primitives, \exp(g), -\cos(g), and \sin(g). For each primitive, the proportionality checker (Alg.proportionality?) verifies whether the integrand equals the primitive's derivative times a factor independent of the integration coordinate. If successful, the candidate is that constant factor times the primitive.

Integration by parts. The LIATE heuristic ranks factors by their suitability for differentiation. Logarithmic and inverse-trigonometric factors receive rank 5, algebraic polynomial factors rank 4, trigonometric factors rank 3, and exponential factors rank 2. For a product u \cdot v', the planner recursively integrates v', forms uv - \int u'v, recursively integrates the correction, and validates the result. The initial recursion fuel is 96; this bounds recursive depth, not the total number of calls across search branches.

Exponential-trigonometric recurrences. For integrands of the form e^{ax}(p(x)\sin(cx) + q(x)\cos(cx)), the planner solves a finite coupled polynomial recurrence. Writing the antiderivative as e^{ax}(P(x)\sin(cx) + Q(x)\cos(cx)), the amplitudes satisfy

P' + aP - cQ = p, \qquad Q' + cP + aQ = q.

When a^2 + c^2 \neq 0, the constant matrix is invertible, and repeated matrix inversion lowers the polynomial degree. The process terminates in at most \max(\deg p, \deg q) + 1 steps.

The implemented route allows multivariate rational-polynomial amplitudes, with the other coordinates treated as parameters, and common exponential and trigonometric phases whose slopes in the selected coordinate are rational constants.

Trigonometric powers. The planner proposes primitives for sine and cosine powers with every fixed natural exponent. For positive powers, the phase derivative must simplify to an expression independent of the selected coordinate and different from literal zero. The final certificate records the nonvanishing conditions needed for division. For constant nonzero slope \alpha, the low-power cases include:

  • \int \sin(\alpha x)\,dx = -\cos(\alpha x)/\alpha,

  • \int \cos(\alpha x)\,dx = \sin(\alpha x)/\alpha,

  • \int \sin^2(\alpha x)\,dx = x/2 - \sin(\alpha x)\cos(\alpha x)/(2\alpha),

  • \int \cos^2(\alpha x)\,dx = x/2 + \sin(\alpha x)\cos(\alpha x)/(2\alpha).

Rational function integration. For univariate rational functions p(x)/q(x), the pipeline proceeds in three stages:

  • Polynomial division. Exact sparse Euclidean division separates the improper part: p = s \cdot q + r with \deg r < \deg q. The polynomial quotient s is integrated term by term.

  • Hermite reduction. The proper fraction r/q undergoes Yun square-free decomposition of the denominator. For each repeated factor f^m, the Hermite recurrence lowers the multiplicity by one at each step, producing rational correction terms that do not require logarithms.

  • Elementary transcendental integration. The terminal square-free fraction uses partial-fraction decomposition over the rationals. Linear factors give logarithms. For a quadratic denominator ax^2+bx+c, separate off the logarithmic-derivative part. The remaining primitive uses arctangent when b^2-4ac<0 and real logarithms when b^2-4ac>0.

The rational factor search combines rational-root extraction and exact Kronecker search over Rat; extended Euclid supplies the modular inverses. Irrational scales in quadratic primitives remain exact symbolic square roots.

Bronstein (2005, Chapter 2) gives the rational-integration methods behind these stages. Here they are used in a bounded candidate search, and the accepted primitive's derivative is checked.

Compositional linearity. Sums, differences, negations, and scalar-independent multiples are handled compositionally.

Before a certificate's nonzero conditions reach a proof, a checked compactor collects square-root products, extracts common factors, splits products and powers, normalizes factors, and deduplicates them. Its soundness theorem recovers every raw obligation from the compact list.

Example: integrating a rational function.

Consider \int \frac{2x+3}{(x-1)^2(x+2)}\,dx. The algebra to be checked is

\frac{2x+3}{(x-1)^2(x+2)} =\frac{1}{9(x-1)}+\frac{5}{3(x-1)^2}-\frac{1}{9(x+2)}.

Thus, on any interval avoiding 1 and -2, a candidate primitive is

F(x)=\frac19\log|x-1|-\frac{5}{3(x-1)} -\frac19\log|x+2|.

Differentiating the middle term recovers the repeated pole; differentiating the two logarithms recovers the simple poles. This concrete decomposition explains the roles of the pipeline's stages:

  1. Polynomial division. The numerator has lower degree, so the quotient is zero.

  2. Square-free decomposition. The denominator factors as (x-1)^2(x+2). Yun decomposition identifies (x-1) with multiplicity 2 and (x+2) with multiplicity 1.

  3. Hermite reduction. The recurrence absorbs the repeated factor, producing a rational correction and lowering the denominator to square-free form (x-1)(x+2).

  4. Partial fractions. Modular inverse computation splits the residual into terms with denominators (x-1) and (x+2).

  5. Elementary integration. Each partial fraction c/(x-r) integrates to c\log|x-r|.

  6. Validation. The complete candidate is differentiated symbolically, and the residual is normalized to zero by the checked route. The requirement set records x \neq 1 and x \neq -2.

To use the endpoint formula, the entire closed interval must avoid both poles. Checking only a\ne1,-2 and b\ne1,-2 is insufficient: the endpoints a=0, b=2 pass those tests but enclose the pole at 1. This is why the integral theorem asks for nonvanishing at every point of Set.uIcc a b, while a pointwise derivative theorem asks only at its evaluation point.

10.6.3. Formal Jets and Residual Losses🔗

A residual loss is an ordinary real-valued function, differentiated with the analytic Fréchet derivative. A formal jet instead stores coefficients; identifying them with derivatives requires a separate semantic theorem.

Residual losses are ordinary functions.

A pointwise residual energy is the square of a LinearPDE's totalized residual expression. A sampled loss sums these energies over a finite list of points. Interpreting this objective as a classical PDE loss requires a separate regularity proof for the candidate field. Given a parameterized model \theta \mapsto u_\theta, its objective is the ordinary composition \theta \mapsto \operatorname{sampledLoss}(u_\theta).

    Sum of squared totalized residual expressions over a finite sample.

A zero sampled loss can still miss the equation between sample points. For the one-dimensional equation u'=0 on [0,1], choose an integer N\geq1 and A>0, and set

u(x)=\frac{A}{2\pi N}\bigl(1-\cos(2\pi Nx)\bigr), \qquad r(x)=u'(x)=A\sin(2\pi Nx).

At every grid point x_j=j/N, the residual vanishes, so the sampled squared loss is zero. Between these points its magnitude reaches A, which can be arbitrarily large. The candidate is smooth and even has zero values at both endpoints. A uniform residual enclosure would detect this oscillation; sampling alone cannot. Converting such a uniform enclosure to solution accuracy then needs a stability estimate in the relevant norm.

For a differentiable objective f:E\to\mathbb R on a real Hilbert space, the gradient-descent map is

x^+=x-\eta\,\nabla f(x).

In Euclidean coordinates, the Adam-style map first sets g=\nabla f(x) and computes

\begin{aligned} m^+&=\beta_1m+(1-\beta_1)g,\\ v^+&=\beta_2v+(1-\beta_2)(g\odot g),\\ x_i^+&=x_i-\eta\,\frac{m_i^+}{\sqrt{v_i^+}+\varepsilon}. \end{aligned}

Both are total update functions defined from the analytic gradient. An analytic use of the Adam-style map must separately prove the sign and nonvanishing facts it needs for \sqrt{v_i^+}+\varepsilon.

In applications, sampledLoss builds a real-valued objective from an already defined PDE residual and a finite sample. A gradient step then has the form

\theta_{\mathrm{new}} =\theta-\eta\,\nabla_\theta L(\theta),

with the analytic gradient, so a residual-loss theorem rests on no automatic-differentiation compiler.

Higher-order multivariate jets.

The jet layer uses Mathlib's multivariate formal power series, so variables may be indexed by an arbitrary type \iota rather than only by Fin n.

For a multi-index \alpha:\iota\to_0\mathbb N, an order-N jet is a formal coefficient family J_\alpha. When a separate semantic theorem identifies these coefficients with derivatives, the normalization convention is

J_\alpha(f,x)=\frac{D^\alpha f(x)}{\alpha!}.

Formal products use ordinary power-series convolution:

(JK)_\alpha =\sum_{\beta+\gamma=\alpha}J_\beta K_\gamma.

The order index controls finite extraction and finite formal composition. The underlying representation is a full formal power series: coefficients above the index may be nonzero, and the carrier itself contains no function, base point, differentiability proof, or convergence theorem.

For a Euclidean scalar function f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R, the proposition that a formal jet J represents f to first order at x records

\begin{aligned} &f\text{ is differentiable throughout a neighborhood of }x,\\ &J_0=f(x),\\ &J_{e_i}=\partial_i f(x)\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n). \end{aligned}

The function, point, and jet are parameters of the proposition. Only the value and the first coefficients are constrained.

The expression compiler maps every constructor of the verified real expression language to an arbitrary-order multivariate formal jet. Arithmetic nodes use formal power-series algebra. A unary elementary function is lifted by finite formal composition with coefficients computed from normalized symbolic derivatives of the corresponding one-variable primitive.

Under sufficient differentiability and Taylor-remainder hypotheses, this is the familiar finite composition formula

\sum_{k=0}^{N}\frac{g^{(k)}(f(x))}{k!} \bigl(f(x+h)-f(x)\bigr)^k.

Compilation is algebraically total, but analytic claims retain the original ValidAt conditions. In particular, division requires a nonzero denominator, the real logarithm requires a nonzero argument, and the classical square-root rule requires a positive argument.

Higher coefficients remain formal power-series coefficients unless another theorem identifies their analytic meaning. For example, the exponential jet has fourth coefficient

[h_x^4]\,e^{h_x}=\frac1{4!}=\frac1{24}.

This is a coefficient identity; it does not assert a general higher-order Taylor remainder theorem.

An interval jet assigns a rational interval to each formal multivariate coefficient. Encloses F J means that every coefficient through the declared order lies in its interval:

\deg\alpha\le N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_\alpha\in F_\alpha.

The interval operations are explicit rather than typeclass ring operations. This is necessary because interval multiplication is sound but not distributive.

    If the exact formal jet has first-order calculus semantics, its interval value and gradient enclose the function value and its coordinate derivatives.

    This theorem transfers a pointwise semantic certificate. It does not turn coefficientwise enclosures into uniform bounds over a box.

Constants, coordinate seeding, addition, subtraction, negation, and power-series convolution preserve coefficient enclosures. At positive order, extracting the constant and first coefficients gives interval values and an output-first interval Jacobian for a vector residual. These intervals contain the corresponding exact formal coefficients. For a scalar jet that represents the function to first order, they also enclose its value and partial derivatives. These guarantees hold at a single input point.

These pointwise enclosures can supply data for validated root finding. The Krawczyk certificate proves existence and uniqueness of a zero in a closed ball from Jacobian enclosures that hold throughout the ball, together with self-mapping and strict contraction inequalities; a jet certificate supplies the corresponding data at one point.

Relationship to computer-assisted PDE proofs.

Gómez-Serrano's survey of computer-assisted proofs in PDE describes a pipeline that combines interval arithmetic, high-order automatic differentiation, rigorous quadrature, singular-integral decompositions, validated root finding, and problem-specific analytic estimates. PDEAtlas has checked foundations for several of these layers:

  • exact rational interval arithmetic and scalar elementary-function enclosures;

  • exact symbolic differentiation with explicit analytic domains;

  • arbitrary-index, arbitrary-order exact multivariate jets;

  • polynomial interval-jet algebra and certified residual/Jacobian extraction;

  • closed-ball Krawczyk certificates with interval-matrix residual bounds;

  • Taylor models and derivative-bound automation, chiefly in one real variable;

  • rigorous one-dimensional Simpson and Gauss–Legendre quadrature; and

  • abstract compact-operator, Fredholm, Hilbert-basis, and spectral theory.

The survey's Muskat and SQG results further use principal-value singular-integral splitting, multidimensional interval-Newton solvers, computer-validated spectral gaps, and a quantitative Crandall–Rabinowitz bifurcation argument.

10.6.4. Symbolic PDE Theorem API🔗

To check a proposed heat profile, we hold space fixed while differentiating in time, then hold time fixed while taking the spatial Laplacian. In the library's spacetime coordinates p=(t,x,y), time is coordinate zero, so the calculation is

\partial_0u-\partial_1^2u-\partial_2^2u=0.

For the Gaussian the domain matters, since its formula contains 1/t; the polynomial x^2+y^2+4t has no such restriction. In both cases cas computes the coordinate residual, and the slice-Laplacian theorem identifies the spatial sum with the Laplacian of (x,y)\mapsto u(t,x,y). This is how the calculation enters the ordinary heat-equation predicate.

The remaining examples ask different questions of the same calculus. Harmonic kernels require a punctured domain and a normalization; transport adds prescribed values at time zero; rigid rotation tests a symmetric gradient rather than a scalar Laplacian. Each theorem states which of these properties has been proved.

The field itself can remain abstract. In PDE/Examples/Symbolic/CAS/FluxDerivatives.lean, if u is differentiable at x, u(x)\ne0, and v is a fixed vector, the reciprocal-flux example proves \nabla\cdot(u^{-1}v)(x)=-Du(x)[v]/u(x)^2. Here cas differentiates the scalar reciprocal at u(x), and the general divergence chain rule supplies the dependence on u. Only the stated pointwise hypotheses are needed.

The symbolically represented planar Gaussian ansatz, interpreted as an ordinary spacetime function, has zero heat residual in spacetime coordinates at positive time, and the CAS proves it. With

\Phi(t,x,y)=\frac{\exp\!\left(-(x^2+y^2)/(4t)\right)}{4\pi t},

the linked Lean theorem states

t>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \partial_t\Phi-\partial_x^2\Phi-\partial_y^2\Phi=0

at (t,x,y). The slice-Laplacian identity turns this into the residual predicate \operatorname{SatisfiesPDEProblem}(\operatorname{heatEquation}(\{t>0\}),\Phi). For the analytic kernel that predicate is the Gaussian heat theorem; for the symbolic expression the Lean module derives it in an example.

Proof for Theorem 10.31
uses 0

Write \xi=(x,y) and r^2=x^2+y^2. Differentiating the prefactor 1/(4\pi t) and the exponential gives

\begin{aligned} \Phi_t&=\left(\frac{r^2}{4t^2}-\frac1t\right)\Phi,\\ \Phi_{xx}&=\left(\frac{x^2}{4t^2}-\frac1{2t}\right)\Phi,\qquad \Phi_{yy}=\left(\frac{y^2}{4t^2}-\frac1{2t}\right)\Phi. \end{aligned}

Adding the two spatial derivatives recovers the time derivative. The CAS checks this cancellation. The assumption t>0 discharges its time denominators and the validity conditions needed to interpret both rounds of differentiation; \pi\ne0 handles the constant denominator. The residual bridge then gives the displayed equation for the coordinate partial derivatives.

Positive time also selects the branch on which this formula agrees with the analytic heat kernel, whose definition is zero for t\le0. At the spatial origin the positive-time value is 1/(4\pi t), which grows without bound as t\downarrow0. Thus substituting the definition's value at time zero cannot establish an initial-trace theorem.

Proof for Theorem 10.34
uses 1

For the planar logarithmic expression, Theorem 10.23 transports the checked CAS residual to the analytic Laplacian. The Newtonian core instead reuses the general radial-Laplacian identity: the coefficient k(k+2-n) vanishes at k=1, n=3. Its value bridge identifies the reflected expression with the inverse norm; constant scaling gives the normalized fundamental solution.

Harmonicity away from the pole cannot determine the normalization: every constant multiple of a harmonic profile is still harmonic there. In three dimensions the unit-source normalization is visible in the flux through a sphere of radius r>0:

-\int_{\partial B_r}\nabla\Phi_3\cdot n\,dS =-\left(-\frac{1}{4\pi r^2}\right)4\pi r^2=1.

This calculation explains why the coefficient 1/(4\pi) matters. A distributional identity -\Delta\Phi_3=\delta_0 must account for that flux at the excluded pole, which the pointwise zero-residual theorem does not see.

10.6.4.1. One profile, two equations🔗

The profile u(t,x)=\sin(x-t) solves two different equations. We use it as a small example of the wave and transport interfaces:

\partial_t^2u-\partial_x^2u=0, \qquad \partial_tu+\partial_xu=0, \qquad u(0,x)=\sin x.

The checked examples live in PDE/Examples/Hyperbolic. The wave theorem records the zero residual on all spacetime; the transport theorem also checks the assigned value u(0,x)=\sin x by substitution. That part of its proof is a slice equality, with no limiting argument. The derivative calculation is short: u_t=-\cos(x-t) and u_x=\cos(x-t) cancel, while u_{tt}=u_{xx}=-\sin(x-t).

For the wave calculation, the derivative bridge transfers the symbolic identity to ordinary derivatives. The transport example applies the checked derivative tactic directly to the ordinary function. Both calculations then feed the library's PDE predicates.

We can also integrate the residual. For this profile, the symbolic residual equals the ordinary advective derivative at every point, so their integrals agree on every set and both vanish.

Writing R_{\mathrm{sym}} for the reflected residual and D_bu=\partial_tu+\partial_xu, the example proves

R_{\mathrm{sym}}(p)=D_bu(p),\qquad \int_\Omega R_{\mathrm{sym}}\,dp =\int_\Omega D_bu\,dp,\qquad \int_\Omega D_bu\,dp=0

for every p\in\mathbb R^2 and every set \Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2. A conservation-law weak formulation needs more, including test functions and the initial or boundary terms.
